reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: The commonest benign solid ovarian tumour, arising from ovarian stromal fibroblasts and typically hormonally inactive
Usually presents in middle-aged or older women as an incidental solid adnexal mass or with non-specific pelvic discomfort
Meigs syndrome is the classic association: a benign ovarian fibroma accompanied by ascites and a pleural effusion that both resolve after removal of the tumour
On imaging it appears as a solid, hypoechoic mass with acoustic shadowing on ultrasound and low signal on T2-weighted MRI, reflecting its dense fibrous tissue
When a fibromatous stroma contains a thecal component it is termed a fibrothecoma, which may then be mildly oestrogenic
Multiple or bilateral fibromas in a young patient should raise suspicion of the naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome
Cellular fibromas and the borderline mitotically active variant can occasionally recur, so complete excision and histological review are important
reference.pathophysiology: Ovarian fibromas are benign sex cord-stromal tumours composed of spindle-shaped fibroblasts producing collagen, giving a firm, white, whorled cut surface. They are generally non-functional because they lack the hormone-secreting theca or granulosa elements, although admixture with thecal cells (fibrothecoma) can confer mild oestrogenic activity. In Meigs syndrome, transudation of fluid from the surface of a large fibroma produces ascites, and fluid tracks to the pleural space, most often on the right, generating an effusion; both resolve once the tumour is excised, distinguishing this benign phenomenon from malignant ascites. Rare cellular and mitotically active variants sit at the borderline of behaviour and warrant careful pathological assessment.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic ovarian tumour such as Krukenberg
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a solid, shadowing ovarian mass
Pelvic MRI to characterise a fibrous lesion with low T2 signal
Chest imaging if a pleural effusion suggests Meigs syndrome
CA125 (which may be mildly raised in Meigs syndrome despite benign disease) and other markers to help exclude malignancy
Histology to confirm the diagnosis and identify cellular or mitotically active variants
Consideration of genetic assessment for Gorlin syndrome in young or multifocal cases
redFlags: A solid ovarian mass with ascites, which requires distinction of benign Meigs syndrome from ovarian carcinoma
Rapid growth or solid vascular components suggesting a more aggressive lesion
Bilateral or multiple fibromas in a young patient, prompting evaluation for Gorlin syndrome
Acute pain from torsion of a pedunculated mass
reference.prognosis: Excellent, as fibromas are benign and cured by excision, with ascites and effusion resolving after removal in Meigs syndrome; only rare cellular or mitotically active variants carry a small risk of recurrence.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting a fibroma with ascites and a raised CA125 as ovarian cancer and overtreating
Confusing a solid ovarian fibroma with a pedunculated uterine fibroid on imaging
Overlooking Gorlin syndrome when fibromas are bilateral or occur in the young
Failing to recognise cellular or mitotically active variants that may recur
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Ovarian fibroma is benign, so management is surgical rather than staged oncologic therapy: confirm the mass is benign, remove it, and confirm the diagnosis on histology.
In women past reproductive plans with an imaging-typical solid adnexal mass, oophorectomy or salpingo-oophorectomy is generally curative.

In younger women wishing to preserve fertility, ovary-sparing tumourectomy or cystectomy is a reasonable alternative provided enough normal ovarian tissue remains and the specimen goes to full histology.
Torsion of a pedunculated fibroma is a surgical emergency managed by urgent detorsion or excision on the standard adnexal torsion pathway.

Meigs syndrome (fibroma with ascites and usually right-sided pleural effusion) is managed by excising the fibroma, after which the effusion and ascites resolve; a large symptomatic effusion can be drained for symptomatic relief while surgery is arranged, but it is not treated as malignant disease.

Cellular or mitotically active/borderline fibroma variants are managed with complete surgical excision as for typical fibroma, with closer histological review and clinical follow-up given a small recognised risk of local recurrence.

Surgery is the sole definitive treatment; there is no established role for radiotherapy or systemic chemotherapy or hormonal therapy in ovarian fibroma, in contrast to the malignant sex cord-stromal tumours (granulosa cell and Sertoli-Leydig tumours) which do receive systemic therapy.

Preoperative work-up includes transvaginal ultrasound and pelvic MRI to characterise the mass as solid and fibrous, tumour markers including CA125 (which can be mildly elevated in Meigs syndrome despite benign disease), and chest imaging if a pleural effusion is present.
After histology confirms an ordinary benign fibroma, no oncologic surveillance is needed beyond routine gynaecologic follow-up since excision is curative.
Cellular or mitotically active/borderline fibromas warrant a period of clinical follow-up for their small recurrence potential.

Bilateral or multiple fibromas, especially in a young patient, should prompt genetic referral for evaluation of naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome rather than repeat ovarian imaging surveillance.

Refer to gynaecologic oncology when imaging shows a solid ovarian mass with ascites and an equivocal or rising CA125, since distinguishing Meigs syndrome from ovarian malignancy with ascites is the key clinical risk.
Refer for genetic counselling when fibromas are bilateral, multiple, or occur in a young patient to evaluate for Gorlin syndrome.
Refer urgently for surgery in suspected torsion of a pedunculated fibroma.
